Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of tasks. However, their performance often degrades in highly specialized domains that require precise structural reasoning, consistency, and domain-specific knowledge. In electronic hardware design, existing LLMs struggle with the structural and semantic complexity of circuit descriptions. Hardware designs are represented as interconnected graphs, including netlists, schematics, and hierarchical design projects. These representations carry essential information that is lost when converted into purely […] quential text.
 As a part of our team, you will research novel methods for adapting generative AI systems to specialized domains by integrating structured symbolic knowledge, without relying on extensive model retraining.
 Your investigation will focus on mechanisms that enable Large Language Models (LLMs) and other foundation models to leverage external knowledge representations such as knowledge graphs, ontologies, and formal design representations while preserving the reasoning capabilities of symbolic systems.

How to avoid learning too much - safe and efficient learning for control 
 Job description 
Inefficient operation of industrial systems, electricity production, and heating systems in buildings is currently responsible for over 50% of overall greenhouse gases emissions. Improving energy efficiency of energy-intensive sectors by implementing advanced control systems has the potential to both improve efficiency and reduce the costs, all while continuing to meet safety requirements. The flexibility of safe and adaptive learning control methods makes them crucial for safety-critical applications. […] requirements. The flexibility of safe and adaptive learning control methods makes them crucial for safety-critical applications. A key difficulty in these learning-based approaches lies in the fact that the algorithm must simultaneously learn the model and guarantee safety. This dual requirement significantly impacts the computational cost of the learning algorithm, particularly in situations where the optimal decision evolves over time. We now aim to develop computationally efficient safe learning methods for time-varying optimal control problems.
Existing safe learning algorithms usually assume that they have unlimited access to the experiments and thus unlimited new data. Approaches using limited data sets have been restricted to Bayesian optimization without safety constraints. Moreover, the algorithms typically rely on the repetitive nature of the experiments, for instance in robotics or precision manufacturing. The unlimited data combined with repetitiveness limit the applicability of safe learning algorithms in problems evolving over time, such as residential buildings. This PhD project will explore the connection between the dynamics of the optimized system with numerical properties of optimization algorithms to provide a framework for safe learning with minimal interactions over time. More about being a doctoral student at the Faculty of Science at naturvetenskap.se Doctoral studies | Faculty of Science Subject and project description Diffusion MRI (dMRI) measures microscopic properties in the tissue by studying random motion of water molecules. In dense tissue, diffusion is slow, while it appears to be faster in looser tissue. dMRI can therefore detect cancers that cause the tissue to be abnormally dense. However, current dMRI methods are sensitive but not very specific. This shortcoming can be remedied by controlling how the diffusion is encoded by the MRI scanner, thereby allowing us to learn more about the tissue microstructure in the living human body. For example, we aim to distinguish properties like cell density, cell shape, cell size, blood volume, and cell membrane permeability. These parameters are then evaluated as tentative imaging biomarkers for improved diagnostics or monitoring of disease. The present project will focus on developing methods for enhancing and analysing the acquired images. Thermodynamic modelling of minority phases in EAF steels The transition to EAF steelmaking creates challenges for the reliable production of thin rolled steel products where residual element accumulation may compromise processability and properties. This PhD will utilise thermodynamic modelling to obtain predictions of equilibrium and, where possible, non-equilibrium phases for a matrix of compositions covering flat rolled products including elevated levels of Cu, Mo, Ni & Sn. These will be incorporated into machine learning models to predict face formation in EAF steels with elevated residual contents. Direct comparisons will be made with experimentally identified phases from high throughput samples. Subsequent characterisation will be performed using a combination of scanning transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction and, where necessary, synchrotron X-ray diffraction, nano-secondary ion mass spectroscopy, and 3D atom probe tomography. The data acquired will be used to modify thermodynamic database parameters to improve the predictions.
